title: Imagining Python versus reading Python
takeaway: An instruction to imagine that a JavaScript snippet is Python pushes the token python high in the J-lens readout at the snippet's own tokens, while a probe for Python-ness with its J-space part removed stays at its no-instruction baseline. Real Python code moves that probe by three to six standard deviations, and only sometimes moves the lens. The paper reads the pair of results as evidence that the instruction writes to the workspace rather than re-encoding the stimulus.
walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image, and it has two halves.

The left half is a single worked example, titled "Example: imagining JavaScript code is Python". At the top sits the prompt: the instruction "Imagine that the following code is written in Python.", followed by a JavaScript function with one token boxed. Beneath it are three columns of [[j-lens-readout]]s taken at that boxed token, at layer 62. Layer numbers here are percentages of depth, so 62 falls inside the workspace band of [[layer-bands]], roughly L38 to L92. Each column lists the five highest-scoring vocabulary tokens with their log probability, and each bar's length is that token's probability relative to the column's own top token. The rank of python in the full readout is printed alongside.

The three columns are three conditions: a neutral instruction, the imagine instruction, and a matched snippet of real Python code. Under each column a gauge carries one further number, written as a signed z-score in units of $\sigma$: the value of a Python-code probe with its J-space component removed.

That probe is the control the experiment turns on. It is a [[linear-probe]] built as the mean difference of activations on real positive and negative stimuli. Its [[j-space-component]] is then projected out, using the top $k=25$ J-lens directions found by [[gradient-pursuit]], so what remains reads only the part of the representation lying outside the workspace. The paper calls the result a [[j-orthogonalized-property-probe]].

The right half, titled "Across four properties", aggregates the same two measures over four stimulus categories with 24 stimuli each: coding language, verb tense, part of speech, capitalization. Two stacked bar panels share one vertical axis in z-scores against the no-instruction baseline. The upper panel gives the effect of the imagine instruction; the lower gives the effect of a real stimulus that genuinely has the property. Each category carries two bars, one per measure, with dots for individual stimuli and error bars of $\pm 1$ SEM over stimuli.

The reported pattern is a dissociation. The instruction raises the property's name in the lens by several standard deviations while leaving the probe within roughly one standard deviation of baseline in every category. A real stimulus moves the probe by three to six standard deviations, and moves the lens in some categories but not all.

The reverse case appears too. A past-tense sentence drives the tense probe up six standard deviations while past stays far down the lens ranking, which the paper takes as a property represented and used without its label entering the [[j-space]] — the distinction section 3.5 develops as [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]].

terms.definition: The instruction under test, here "Imagine that the following code is written in Python." It asks the model to treat the stimulus as having a property the stimulus does not actually have.
The text the instruction is applied to: in the example, a JavaScript function. It genuinely has the original property (JavaScript) and not the imagined one (Python).
The single token inside the carrier at which the lens readout in the example is taken. Measurements in the aggregate panels are averaged over all stimulus token positions instead.
The five highest-scoring vocabulary tokens of the Jacobian-lens readout at that position and layer. The lens scores every token by how strongly the activation encodes the potential to verbalize it.
The units of the numbers printed beside each lens token. The bar drawn for a token is its probability relative to the top token of the same column, so the top row is always full width.
The depth at which the example readout is taken. The paper reports 25 evenly spaced layers reindexed to a 0-100 scale, so 62 means 62% of the way through the model.
The position of the token python in the full vocabulary-wide readout for that column, printed even when python does not make the visible top five.
The baseline condition: the same JavaScript carrier with no instruction to imagine anything. It fixes what the lens and the probe read with the stimulus alone.
The positive control: a matched snippet of code that genuinely is Python, read under a neutral instruction. It shows what both measures look like when the property is actually present.
The second measure, and one of the two legend entries. A linear probe for the property whose J-space part has been projected out, so it reads the property only from directions outside the workspace.

terms.term: J-lens activation of tokens naming the property
terms.definition: The first measure, and the other legend entry. It is how strongly the lens scores the token that names the property - python, past, verb, caps - at the stimulus positions.

The four property-naming tokens, one per category. The lens measure tracks these tokens specifically; the probe never sees them, since it is a direction in activation space rather than a vocabulary entry.
How the probe direction is constructed: the average activation on stimuli that have the property minus the average on stimuli that do not.
The step that makes the probe a control. The activation's nearest point in the J-space is subtracted, so any movement the probe reports comes from outside the workspace.
The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm used to pick the J-lens directions that reconstruct the activation, here the top 25 of them.
The band of middle layers, about L38 to L92, in which the paper argues the J-space behaves like a workspace. Both measures are averaged over this band.
One of the four stimulus categories: a JavaScript snippet, with the instruction to imagine it is Python.
A present-tense sentence, with the instruction to imagine it is past tense. Its property-naming token is past.
A noun, with the instruction to imagine it is a verb. Its property-naming token is verb.
A lowercase word, with the instruction to imagine it is in all caps. Its property-naming token is caps.

The vertical axis of both bar panels: the shift in a measure relative to the no-instruction baseline, expressed in standard deviations of that measure. It puts the lens score and the probe value on one comparable scale.
The effect of the imagine instruction on each measure, per category. This is the condition where the model is asked to treat the stimulus as something it is not.
The same two measures for a matched stimulus that genuinely has the property. It shows what a real change in the input does, as a reference for the upper panel.
Vertical bars of plus or minus one standard error of the mean, computed across the stimuli within a category.
Individual stimuli, jittered within each bar. They show the spread behind each mean rather than only its summary.
The reference condition both panels are scored against: the original stimulus with no imagine instruction and no property swap.
The region of representation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues acts as the model's workspace. The probe is built to exclude it.

numbers.meaning: Stimulus categories: coding language, verb tense, part of speech, capitalization. Four were chosen so the result does not rest on the Python example alone, and they span code, syntax, morphology and surface form.
Stimuli per category (n=24), giving the dots and the standard-error bars in each bar. It is the sample the means and SEMs are computed over.
Columns in the left-hand example: neutral instruction, imagine instruction, real Python. Three are needed because the imagine condition has to be read against both a floor and a ceiling.
Lens tokens shown per column (top-5). It is a display cutoff only; the rank of python is reported from the full readout, which is why that rank can exceed 5.
The layer of the example readout, on the paper's 0-100 reindexing of depth. It sits inside the workspace band, where the J-space is claimed to carry abstract content.
The number of J-lens directions (k=25) removed from the probe by gradient pursuit. It matches the paper's measured J-space occupancy, which plateaus around 25 concepts across the workspace band.
The approximate start and end of the workspace layer band, on the 0-100 depth scale, over which both measures are averaged. Section 4.1 locates this band with four separate lens statistics.
The scale layer numbers are reindexed to, from 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, so a layer number reads as a percentage of the model's depth.
The error bars are plus or minus one standard error of the mean over stimuli - the narrower convention, not a 95% interval.
Measures per category, drawn as two bars: the J-lens activation of the property-naming token, and the J-orthogonalized property probe. The whole figure is the contrast between them.
The typical size of the imagine instruction's effect on the J-lens measure. The paper does not give one number for it, since it varies by category.
The bound the paper gives on the imagine instruction's effect on the J-orthogonalized probe, in every category. It is the sense in which the probe is described as unmoved.
How far a real positive stimulus moves the J-orthogonalized probe. This range is what establishes that the probe is sensitive enough to have detected a re-encoding, had one occurred.
The tense probe's response to a genuinely past-tense sentence, in the case where past nonetheless stays far down the lens ranking. It is the paper's example of the dissociation running the other way.
